reference.source: Rook's Textbook of Dermatology / Fitzpatrick's Dermatology
clinicalPearls: An acquired autoimmune subepidermal blistering disease caused by autoantibodies to type-VII collagen, the major component of anchoring fibrils
The classic mechanobullous form produces skin-fragile, non-inflammatory tense blisters at trauma-prone sites (hands, feet, elbows, knees) that heal with scarring and milia
An inflammatory form can closely mimic bullous pemphigoid, mucous membrane pemphigoid, or linear IgA disease
Because anchoring fibrils are lost, healing may leave scarring, milia, and nail dystrophy, echoing inherited dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa
Salt-split skin immunofluorescence localises IgG to the dermal (floor) side of the split, in contrast to bullous pemphigoid which binds the epidermal roof
Associations with inflammatory bowel disease, particularly Crohn disease, are recognised
It is characteristically treatment-resistant compared with bullous pemphigoid
reference.pathophysiology: Epidermolysis bullosa acquisita is mediated by IgG (and sometimes IgA) autoantibodies against type-VII collagen, the structural protein of the anchoring fibrils that tether the epidermal basement membrane to the papillary dermis. Antibody binding beneath the lamina densa impairs dermo-epidermal adhesion; in the mechanobullous form this produces fragile skin that blisters with minor trauma, whereas complement activation and inflammatory cell recruitment drive the inflammatory variants. Because the cleavage plane lies below the lamina densa and anchoring fibrils are damaged, healing is often accompanied by scarring and milia, mirroring hereditary dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa.
additionalInvestigations: Perilesional biopsy for direct immunofluorescence showing linear IgG/C3 at the basement membrane zone
Salt-split skin immunofluorescence to localise binding to the dermal floor
Serum indirect immunofluorescence and ELISA for anti-type-VII collagen antibodies
Lesional histology confirming a subepidermal blister
Screening for inflammatory bowel disease when gastrointestinal symptoms are present
Porphyrin studies to exclude porphyria cutanea tarda in acral bullous disease
redFlags: Mucosal or ocular scarring threatening function and vision
Oesophageal or laryngeal involvement causing dysphagia or airway compromise
Progressive disease refractory to standard immunosuppression
reference.prognosis: Epidermolysis bullosa acquisita tends to run a chronic, relapsing course and is often refractory to treatment; scarring, milia, and functional impairment from mucosal disease can accumulate over time.
pitfalls: Diagnosing bullous pemphigoid without a salt-split skin study to identify dermal-side binding
Underestimating scarring and mucosal complications, including ocular disease
Confusing acral blistering with porphyria cutanea tarda
Expecting a prompt response to therapy when the disease is characteristically resistant
management: Suppress the autoantibody response against type-VII collagen with systemic corticosteroids combined with steroid-sparing agents such as colchicine, dapsone, ciclosporin, azathioprine or mycophenolate mofetil
Escalate refractory or severe disease to rituximab or intravenous immunoglobulin
Protect skin in the mechanobullous form with trauma avoidance and non-adherent dressings, and provide wound care for erosions, milia and scarring
Manage mucosal involvement, including ocular, oral and oesophageal disease, with appropriate specialist input and stricture dilatation
Screen for and treat associated inflammatory bowel disease, particularly Crohn disease
Monitor for treatment-related toxicity from prolonged immunosuppression
Refer to dermatology for coordinated long-term care of this chronic relapsing disease
